title: Proposition 1 (bounded search) omits the explicit upper bound on z needed for finiteness

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
Proposition 1 claims no solution with $\max x_i\le 120$, proved by a finite search. I independently re-ran the exhaustive search over $1\le x_1\le\cdots\le x_5\le 120$ and confirmed there is NO solution, so the assertion is correct.

However, the proof never states the upper bound on $z$ that makes the search loop finite. Given $\max x_i\le 120$, one has $z^6=\sum x_i^6\le 5\cdot 120^6$, hence $z\le \lfloor 120\cdot 5^{1/6}\rfloor = 158$. The write-up only says 'one checks each sixth power $z^6\ge x_5^6+2s_1$' (a lower bound) and never bounds $z$ from above. For rigor the proof must state $z\le 158$. Minor exposition gap, not a mathematical error.

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body: Re-review against the current solution.tex (N=220 revision): this gap is now ADDRESSED. Lemma 1 ('Range of $z$', `lem:zrange`) explicitly proves $z\le z_{\max}=\lfloor(5N^6)^{1/6}\rfloor+2$ via eq. (Zbound) and the two-sided range $s+2x_3^6\le z^6\le s+2N^6$. The finiteness of the search loop is now rigorously justified. Recommend marking resolved.
